I thought that earlier on the Chairman of the committee made a very eloquent appeal for civility in this House. I think there is nothing more important than civility in this House, especially in a debate of this kind. I do not think jeers from Ministers assist that. We have been talking about enhancing the role of the private Member and we have a Minister with nothing better to do than make cheap wisecracks. Nevertheless, I will attempt to continue in the way I started because, in spite of discouraging evidence, I still think most Members in this House are serious about reform. The contemptuous attitude that some individuals show to their colleagues is the exception rather than the rule. Indeed, as the Hon. Member who chaired the committee said, this House will only function well when Members show respect for each other.
When I was first elected in 1974, most matters in this House were agreed on by consensus. We very rarely had the bitter divisions among House Leaders that we have seen since. Again, in spite of what I am seeing opposite me at the moment, in spite of the discourtesy I am seeing across the way at the moment, I still share the hope of the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) that we will return to civility and again have a House where, when we have school children in the galleries, we are not ashamed of what they are seeing but we are proud of what they are seeing.
There are a number of examples of situations where Members on all sides of this House work well together. This happens in committees with subject matter references, for one thing. It also happens in the Standing Committee on Public Accounts which traditionally has operated in a very non-partisan fashion. I am pleased to see a former chairman and a former vice-chairman of that committee in the House today. In committees dealing with Estimates and legislation, the
Standing Orders
attitude has traditionally been confrontational. Some of that is inevitable. However, we can work to reduce unnecessary conflict.
The suggestion put forward that the standing committees hear witnesses and examine the subject matter of a Bill before second reading is an interesting one. If that were implemented I would hope one could get a much more non-partisan understanding of the Bill on second reading, and therefore a better second reading debate. It still might be vigorous debate but at least it will be based on understanding and commitment. At that point, indeed, a legislative committee should be able to do its work very promptly and not need to hear witnesses other than technical witnesses. So the idea of a legislative committee is one which I support, but its implementation needs to be worked out.
Our legislative committees got off to a bad start. There were far too many. For example, before Christmas we had eight sitting at one point. In the British House, where they have 600 Members, I think five is the maximum that can sit at the same time. As well, the legislative committees suddenly came into being but the previous step, where the subject matter of the legislation is examined in the standing committee, had not taken place. Therefore, there were many angry exchanges in legislative committees because we suddenly found that witnesses were being cut off but we had not really had an opportunity to test the pulse of the public. However, those are administrative matters which can be dealt with, given some goodwill and some care.
To turn to some of the other changes in this motion before us, one very positive factor is the review of delegated legislation. There are a lot of good opportunities there for serious Members to do some good work.
The 45-day limit for answers to a certain number of written questions is good. It puts some pressure on the Government to take seriously Members' questions, and in those circumstances setting a limit to the number of questions on the Order Paper from a Member at a given time is also reasonable.
The supply debate I think can be expected to go better based on this motion before us because the fact that the Leader of the Opposition can concentrate on the Estimates of one Department might make for a very much more intensive and careful examination. I think examining expenditures is an extremely important part of the work of this House. It is important for democracy. The more that Parliament really shows that it cares about control of the public purse and that the executive of the day cannot just write blank cheques, the more faith the public will have in our efforts to ensure that their tax moneys are spent wisely. Control by Parliament should be not just words mouthed by politicians, but should be a very real experience if the role of the Member of Parliament is to count and if people are to have confidence in the fact that we take seriously the fact that they work hard for their money and are entitled to know where it goes.
The new rules about Private Members' Bills are interesting. They will also need some working out. We will have to be very clear about how the five-hour debate is managed. Again, that

Standing Orders
is a relatively small administrative matter which can be dealt with.
The reduction of statements under Standing Order 22 from 90 seconds to 60 seconds is good because it allows more people to participate.
The final matter I would like to comment on is something that is not in the motion before us but was a recommendation of the committee, that is, the proposal that the written questions about the Estimates could be put forward by a standing committee and that answers to the committee would be back before May 1st. The written material could then be used by members in committee. That is a very interesting proposal. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to make some brief comments with respect to this motion to amend the Standing Orders of the House. There are a great number of very significant changes being brought forth and an enormous amount of credit goes directly to the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and his outstanding committee for their hard work and effort in preparing the report on which these amendments are based.
I also want to add my own personal congratulations to the Chairman and the members of the committee for that fine work.
These amendments are particularly significant to Members of Parliament and private Members specifically. Hopefully we will find that they are significant to the general public as well. I suspect that at this stage the significance of these amendments will be lost to the Canadian people generally, but there is one particular aspect of these amendments for which the people of this country have long been looking. Those are the amendments with respect to the review of Order in Council appointments. This review process is long overdue. It was a significant issue in the election campaign of 1984 and is an issue of concern to the general public who believed that there needed to be a significant and substantial change to the process by which Order in Council appointments are made.
I believe it is to the Government's credit and particularly to the credit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that action was taken virtually immediately upon the calling of the Thirty-third Session of Parliament in November, 1984.
The House will recall that there was reference to setting up a task force on parliamentary reform in the Speech from the Throne and subsequently the task force was put in place. The task force came up with recommendations upon which these amendments are based and the Government responded and substantially adopted the recommendations that were made by that committee.
Today, we are about to implement a review of Order in Council appointments with the exception of judicial appointments.
I suggest most Members have heard complaints from the public since September 4, 1984, about what has happened to the appointment process. The public was anxious to see quick action with new procedures being put into place and could not understand why it was taking so long or that there was any delay at all.
The changes that I trust will be implemented this afternoon are revolutionary to the whole sense of our parliamentary system. The fact is that no change like this has ever taken place in the British parliamentary system and it is the first time that there has been a review process for Order in Council appointments or any federal government appointments.
Of course, the Americans have a type of review process. They review federal judicial appointments through their Senate committee and a requirement under their Constitution for the advice and consent of the Senate when the President makes those appointments. They also have confirmation hearings for members of the federal Cabinet in the United States. However, there is no similar process where all types of appointments made by the American federal Government can be reviewed. Therefore, not only are these changes revolutionary as far as the British parliamentary system is concerned, I believe they are revolutionary as far as democracy is concerned.
These changes will not as yet require a review of all appointments. For instance, judicial appointments do not require this review. The House may recall that last week I introduced in the House a Private Member's Bill calling for a
February 12, 1986

procedure for the review of federal judicial appointments. That Bill was talked out at the time, but 1 am hopeful that we will see some form of recognition of that process as well.
However, the fact that we are implementing a form of review for the first time is a most significant step. While this form of review and its implementation may not please everyone, I hope that it represents one more step in the process of improving the concept of the review of appointments.
Perhaps we could consider some of the review processes that are used municipally in this country. For example, efforts are made to try to make appointments accessible for everyone in an attempt to ensure that people with the highest qualifications are chosen for those jobs. In some cases, there is a process for advertising openings and vacancies on boards, commissions and committees. There is a process for making written applications where a review panel or board considers those applications and makes a short list. That review panel conducts advance interviews according to that short list and makes recommendations to a municipal council which accepts or rejects that recommendation. I believe that is a good process that could be adopted, at least in part, for our parliamentary system in the future.
I want to emphasize that these changes represent a revolution by evolution. It is a gigantic step forward because it is the first time in British parliamentary history that any sort of review process has been put in place. It is a great tribute to the Hon. Member for St. John's East and his colleagues in the committee. It is a tribute to the Government and particularly to the Prime Minister without whose unfailing support we would not have this process. I suggest that in future, as the public learns to appreciate and understand this process, it will be one of the hallmarks of the present Government's years in office.

Mr. Speaker, just for the purpose of historical accuracy, I am somewhat surprised that the Hon. Member said that this is the first time in the history of Canada that we have had such a review. Is he familiar with a review chaired by the former Member of Parliament from Pontiac-Gatineau, Tom Lefebvre? This was begun and struck by the Liberal Government in 1982.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's comments. When I was referring to a parliamentary review process, I was not referring to the committee which looked into the question of reforming the rules or the Standing Orders of the House, but rather to the fact that we are setting in place today, I hope, a process whereby Government appointments to boards and commissions etc. will be reviewed by a parliamentary committee. That has never happened before. It may have been recommended before, but it has never been put in place before.
That is the historic fact we are witnessing here today and one which we should all applaud.
Standing Orders

Mr. Speaker, let me begin my analysis of the situation by saying that I would hate to think I am a little more cynical than some of my senior colleagues, but in looking at the whole process of parliamentary reform it seems there has been an issue not addressed in the debate today, that of the role of the private Member, specifically in a parliamentary democracy.
As long as we have a Cabinet and a Parliament which derives the majority of its responsibility through Cabinet decisions, most of them made by the so-called P and P Committee or the inner Cabinet, any discussion of expanding the private Member's role in committee, expanding funding capabilities for private Members, expanding study possibilities for private Members, while on the surface bears further study and deserves support, lends a false sense of the role of a private Member to the public at large.
I think it is pretty clear that as long as we remain in a parliamentary system where the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and the Cabinet are the bottom line, no matter how many committees we strike, how much money we give the chairmen, how much we open up the process through TV or through other mechanisms to allow the public to see the workings of the House, until we change the fundamental principle of Cabinet responsibility and ministerial responsibility that has been based on the traditional British system, most of these so-called reforms will merely become a House of cards. I refer specifically to the particular motion the Member just discussed with respect to review of appointments.
The Government, embarrassed as it was, by the profligate numbers of appointments made in its first year of Government, particularly in light of the Prime Minister's own self-confessed virginity on this issue during the political debates, has come forward with a position paper which says that ordinary Members will now have a chance to review every Order in Council appointment.
There are prescriptions however, Mr. Speaker. Members must review appointments within 30 days of their being recorded in Hansard. We know that if the appointments continue at the rate we saw in the fall of 1984 and the spring of 1985, it will be very difficult for Members to review all those appointments within the prescribed 30 days period.
The committee however, is powerless, the committee is neutered when it comes to doing anything about inappropriate appointments. I think this goes beyond the partisan political issue because previous Liberal Cabinets were not prepared and the current Conservative Cabinet is still not prepared to relinquish any of its bottom line authority and power.
What we are talking about is developing a system to permit private Members on all sides of the House not only to put more into the process but to begin to wield more influence in the decision-making of Government.
Particularly in a majority Government system we know that unless we move away from the notion of a Cabinet, unless we move toward a kind of Congressional system as we see in the United States, and if we move away from the notion of caucus

February 12, 1986
Standing Orders
solidarity, we will forever be creating committees which may have the power to issue a press release, the power to hire a researcher, but the substantive power of those committees is lost in the Cabinet shuffle.
I think about the committee on day care which was announced with much fanfare by the Government just this last week. We know the Government is spending $1 million to send parliamentarians across the country to look at a very critical issue, the issue of day care. It looks good. The Government says that it is spending $1 million because it is concerned about the issue.
But let us look at the fisheries committee. I gather its budget was in the neighbourhood of half a million dollars. That committee travelled across Canada. It took presentations from fishermen and people in the field. Committee members spent many hours in the community and came back with what is considered to be a reasonably good report. Yet on the most important issue facing the fisheries committee, the issue of factory freezer trawlers, the decision was not made by the committee, the decision was not made by the people who travelled across the country to hear hundreds of presentations, the decision was made by the Cabinet without even waiting to hear the results of the committee's work.
We can, however, diffuse our efforts. We can set up 28 standing committees with a minimum of five and a maximum of 7 or 11 members, but if we remain in the confines of a parliamentary system that sees the Cabinet with its ministerial budget and ministerial power, and as long as we do not have private Member all-Party input into the Priorities and Planning Committee, then any motion of expanding the role of the private Member by mere tinkering with the parliamentary system is illusory.
I have only worked as an Opposition Member both in the Ontario Legislature and in the federal House. I think that Members on all sides of the House who presented this report and who did the work are very sincere. I think they are seeking a chance for the private Member to have a greater involvement in the process. I can appreciate, particularly on the Government side with its very large majority, that many Members are frustrated. They may feel that their work is not recognized and that the hours they spend in committee are often ignored by the public and their peers.
I would suggest that if we are truly concerned about parliamentary reform, we must attack the issue at its heart, namely, on the question of Cabinet responsibility. When we tell a committee that it has the power to review Order in Council appointments, that power must not simply be window dressing with more budgets, more time and more television coverage. That the power must say to the committee: "We, the Parliament of Canada, vest in you the capability to say yea or nay. You are the bottom line. You are the seal of approval". Cabinet and the Prime Minister make the recommendations. They suggest an Order in Council appointment, but it is ultimately the Parliament of Canada, in majority or minority, through committees, that has an opportunity to have the final say.
Without that particular final authority and without the veto power that was suggested by the committee, the Government has effectively neutered what could have been a very useful tool in the process of parliamentary review.
I have a number of other concerns and I believe that these should be shared by all Members. There may be times in the future when Government Members will be sitting in opposition. They may want to look at the issue from an opposition perspective or they may want to look at it from the perspective of the protection of the rights of the individual Member, but I am extremely concerned about two particular motions as they relate to the so-called naming of Members.
We are suggesting that in the next Parliament we will have the election of a Speaker, which is not the case at the moment, although we have a sort of measure by which we can approve the selection made by the Prime Minister. Without a secret ballot selection of a Speaker, what we are saying in this motion is that the Speaker is now invested with the power of being able to name any Member and being able to eject a Member from the House without calling for a motion from the appropriate source. In other words, Mr. Speaker, it is not the Parliament that ultimately becomes the arbiter of what is right and wrong in the House in terms of a vote, it is simply the Speaker, who is an unelected person, who has been appointed by the Prime Minister without the process, as suggested by this committee for an elected secret ballot vote.
I agree that if we had a secret ballot vote there would be some recourse whereby we could say to the Speaker: "You have an opportunity for a naming in an instance", but I would also suggest that not only are we investing in that same Speaker the opportunity to name an individual without a vote in this House, without an opportunity to seek the consent of the Members, whose job it is not only to keep this place orderly but to keep the debate going, but the Speaker has been given the opportunity or the responsibility of naming a Member for up to a week at a time.
It seems that when we are talking about an ejection of five days' duration, and when we are talking about cutting off not only that Member but the constituents of the particular riding, we are denying them an opportunity to have a voice in Parliament for a whole week. It could be the week following the Budget. It could be the most important decision-making week in Canada. It could have been the week of the Constitution. Not only is the Member denied the opportunity to participate, but the constituency and its hundred thousand voters are being told that they cannot have a say for a week, and that decision will be made by a Speaker who at the moment is not elected in a democratic form by the House.
I suggest that the particular measure is punitive. I do not think it is in the best interest of any Member, including Government Members, to vest that in the Speaker alone with no recourse or suggestion that Parliament move a motion. We are small numbers in the Opposition. Chances are that if a motion were moved today by the Government House Leader to
February 12, 1986

have the Hon. Member for Hamilton East ejected, the motion would probably pass. It should not, but I suspect it would probably pass. However, in that case the responsibility for the naming becomes the responsibility of the mover of the motion. It becomes the responsibility of Parliament and the democratic process in which every Member of the House-211 Conservatives, 40 Liberals and 30 New Democrats-can stand up and say: "we choose to keep that Member within our ranks" or "we choose to eject that Member". As a result of this particular motion, not only does the Speaker have the authority to eject once but he has the authority to eject a Member for five days.
I think mention has been made of the translation problems in that the English version of the particular motion suggests a five-day suspension for all subsequent so-called namings, but in the French version there is confusion because it only speaks of a second naming. Something must be done to change the Bill in that particular regard.
We believe in Parliament. Parliament is the seat of democracy. At the bottom line should be the motion being moved either by the Government or by the Opposition in other cases. I have very serious concerns about this measure which was not in the McGrath Report. The five-day naming was not an invention of this all-Party committee. It was added by the Government in this particular motion. I find it excessive, I find it punitive, and I think it is not the kind of responsibility which should be accorded a Speaker, particularly when in this Parliament we still have a Speaker who is not elected by secret ballot.
I have some other concerns about the issue of petitions and Order Paper questions. Each of us is here to represent our ridings. There have been a number of suggestions that the number of petitioners must rest at a minimum of 25 for a petition to be valid in the Parliament of Canada and that anything less than 25 is not acceptable for the purposes of petitions. It has also been suggested that because of the overabundance, I guess, of Order Paper questions-although it seems to me that there are not that many questions in relation to the number of Members in the House-we should somehow be restricted in the number of questions we can ask. I am not sure of the number; I think it is four questions per session which we will be allowed to put on the Order Paper as a result of this particular measure.
At any one time.

In any case, it seems that these particular issues-the first being a minimum of 25 voters on the petition and the second being the maximum of Order Paper questions being allowed at any time-are an infringement upon the ability of the ordinary Member to get to the bottom of an issue. It may not be an earth-shattering issue. It may be a local question about the status of the Hamilton Airport. It may in fact be a small petition because there may not have been hundreds of thousands of Canadians rising up on the issue. However, if I receive a petition from 17 members of a senior citizens' club, which has a total membership of 20, those senior
Standing Orders
citizens have every right to petition Parliament through their Member.
I am not sure whether the committee was confronted with overpowering evidence about excessive petitions or whether the committee was presented with overpowering evidence about excessive Order Paper questions. It seems to me that if we look at the Order Paper, most Members only ask one or two questions at a time. In fact, oftentimes those questions are not answered. I know the committee Chairman will say that as a result of this particular provision we will get answers quicker. Well, I lived in a Parliament which required automatic answers to Order Paper questions. If the House thinks that that will be the panacea for getting information, I can tell it that it is not. Essentially what happens is that if the Minister, the Cabinet, the Government, the seat of responsibility and the seat of power, do not want to answer the question, they bring back an answer within the prescribed two-week period which may just be a regurgitation of the question put another way to satisfy the provisions of the Standing Orders.
I return to the point that if we are truly concerned about parliamentary reform, we have to look for reform, for change and for a new direction in the heart of the organism, which is Cabinet. Far be it from me to belittle the work done by committees.

We are now in a situation where the Liberal Party has only 40 Members. We know that with these new provisions and even those to which our Party agreed to for a temporary period, we find ourselves in an impossible situation. There are 28 committees on which, according to the new provisions, we should have not only one representative but also five substitute Members named by that representative. Given all those committees, if our Member does not name five substitute Members within a certain delay, he or she will no longer be entitled to sit on that committee.
Now let us see how these figures work out in the case of the Liberal Party: we have 40 Members, there are 28 committees, each with one Member and five substitutes, so what is 28 times 6? As you can see we would need at least a hundred-odd Members just to assume our committee responsibilities.
Sure enough, Mr. Speaker, there will be no problem after the next election, but we have to face the reality of 1986!
Mr. Speaker, Government Members might be well advised to consider the situation. They have no worries now with their 211 seats, but they should not forget that after the next election the situation might be reversed.
Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that my responsibility is to represent my constituents and I think it would be better to have fewer committees whose responsibilities and reports would be accepted by Cabinet. I am not interested . . . Even last week I was on the labour committee which is a sub-committee of a sub-committee. We got together to consider the question of part-time and shared work. One of the Members of

Standing Orders
the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), said-and I shared his views-that he had no intention of sitting and studying the question of shared work if there were only four or five of us on the committee and if we did not have any assurance that our reports would be accepted by the Government. I would have liked to see fewer committees, but at least some kind of Cabinet guarantee that committees will be struck in a non-partisan manner. For instance we might have six or seven committees, six large committees to study six of the major issues in Canada today, be it employment, structural changes to our employment system, environment, whatever, we should select specific and wide-ranging subjects, major issues in this country, and those committees would have a Cabinet guarantee that their recommendations will be accepted and implemented through legislation. But if there is not going to be any change as far as Cabinet is concerned, then all we are doing here is supposedly meant to improve conditions for Hon. Members of the Opposition parties as well as the Government. But all things considered there will be no meaningful changes, we will continue to operate within the parliamentary system. If we are prepared to make changes, is that really what we are doing? Certainly not with the kind of cosmetic changes proposed in the document under consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I think we have made considerable progress on the debate yesterday and today.
